paragraphs.text: Recent literature and clinical experience have demonstrated that gender identity, described as one’s inner sense of self as male, female, or other nonbinary category, exists as a contin uum between maleness and femaleness. Furthermore, there is increasing evidence that gender identity is not merely a psychosocial construct but rather an entity governed by complex interactions among biology, environ ment, and culture. Gender identity is distinct from sex, the latter of which is categorized based on chromosomal and apparent physical characteristics such as genitalia. The general practice has been to assign sex at birth—and therefore, gender of rearing—based on phe notype, but growing awareness of potential discordance between the body and gender identity has transformed our understanding of what truly governs gender identity [1].
paragraphs.heading: 39.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: Transgender may be defined as a condition where one’s gender identity is not aligned or “congruent” with one’s physical sex character istics. Gender identity may also be nonbinary. Some individuals describe themselves as gen

der expansive, gender fluid, gender queer, or agender. “Cisgender” is a term that is used to describe an individual whose gender identity is in alignment with one’s physical sex charac teristics. It is important to recognize that gen der identity is distinct from sexual identity (sexual orientation). A person with any gen der identity can have any sexual orientation [1].

In 2013, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) removed the diagnosis of “gender identity disorder (GID)” from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Menal Disorders (DSM)-IV and replaced it with “gender dysphoria” in the updated DSM-5, described as a marked incongruence between one’s experienced/expressed gender and assigned gender of at least 6 months duration, which causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning [2]. This change in terminology underscores the con cept that a transgender identity, in and of itself, is no longer considered pathological and, instead, directs clinical concern to the dysphoria that may exist as a consequence of being TGD. It is anticipated that the DSM-6 will replace “gender dysphoria” with “gender incongruence,” acknowledging that not all TGD individuals experience dysphoria, espe cially if well-supported and affirmed in their gender identities.

The size of the TGD youth population is challenging to accurately ascertain, but survey-based studies have estimated that 0.7% to 2.7% of the teenagers in the United States identify as TGD [3–5]. Pediatric gender clinics worldwide have described increased referrals over the years, including the Netherlands [6, 7] and Canada [8].

Gender identity is not simply a psychosocial construct but likely reflects a complex inter play of biology, culture, and environment [1]. Evidence for biological determinants of gen der identity comes from three biomedical dis ciplines such as genetics, endocrinology, and

paragraphs.text: neurology. Of note, the goal in reviewing such studies is not to develop a test to confirm someone’s gender identity nor to identify a mechanism that can be “fixed” to prevent gen der diversity. Rather, it is hoped that an appre ciation that biology contributes to gender identity development can lead to destigamati zation and greater acceptance for gender diverse persons [1].
paragraphs.heading: 39.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: Evidence implicating genetics as a contribut ing factor to gender identity development is derived from studies of twins as well as from studies of polymorphisms in candidate genes that might be more prevalent in transgender persons versus cisgender controls. A literature review in 2012 focused on twins with what was then known as GID [9]. Of 23 pairs of mono zygotic female or male twins, nine pairs (39.1%) were concordant for GID, while there was no concordance for GID in 21 same-sex dizygotic female and male twin pairs or in seven opposite-sex twin pairs [9]. While these studies suggest that DNA does play a role in gender identity development, the fact that concordance for being transgender was only 39.1% in this study of identical twins may reflect epigenetic changes or the fact that indi viduals may “come out” as transgender at any age, even late in life. Studies attempting to identify polymorphisms in candidate genes that might be more prevalent in transgender versus cisgender persons have been inconsis tent. For example, a 2009 study from Japan did not find any significant associations between a transgender identity and polymor phisms in five candidate genes (encoding the androgen receptor, CYP19, ER-α, ER-β, and the progesterone receptor) [10]. However, a 2019 study from the U.S. and Australia in 380 transgender women and 344 cisgender male controls investigated repeat length polymor phisms or single nucleotide polymorphisms in 12 sex hormone signaling genes [11]. In this study, significant associations were identified between gender dysphoria and a number of alleles and genotypes, including an overrepre sentation of several allele combinations
paragraphs.heading: 39.2.1 Genetics

paragraphs.text: involving the androgen receptor in transgen der women [11]. An association between poly morphisms in the estrogen receptor α gene (ESR1) promoter and gender incongruence in transgender males was reported in a 2020 study from Spain [12].
paragraphs.heading: 39.2.1 Genetics

paragraphs.text: While most transgender individuals do not have a difference in sex development (DSD), studies of patients with DSDs support a role of hormones—prenatal (and perhaps postna tal) androgens, in particular—in gender iden tity development. However, the hormonal environment is not likely to be the only deter minant of gender identity, given that most transgender individuals do not have any dis cernable evidence of hormonal abnormalities (though there may have been some variations in prenatal hormone secretion or sensitivity that are not readily apparent from examina tion of the external genitalia).
paragraphs.heading: 39.2.2 Endocrinology

paragraphs.text: Individuals with virilizing congenital adre nal hyperplasia (CAH) represent a population in which the early hormonal environment of 46,XX individuals is largely androgenic, due to various defects in the steroidogenesis path way. Review of the literature has shown that in a case series of 250 46,XX adult individuals with virilizing CAH caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency that were raised female, nearly 95% were identified as females. However, 5.2% had significant gender dysphoria or cross-gender identification, which is significantly higher than the estimated prevalence of female-tomale transgender individuals in the general population [13]. There was, however, no cor relation between degree of genital virilization and gender identity outcome [13]. A study in youth with virilizing 21-hydroxylase-deficient CAH demonstrated that 12.8% of 46,XX individuals demonstrated cross-gender identi fication independent of gender behavior [14]. A variety of other hormonal and nonhor monal DSDs, particularly in 46,XY individu als, support some role of prenatal/postnatal androgens in gender identity development; however, an individual with complete andro gen insensitivity syndrome associated with an
paragraphs.heading: 39.2.2 Endocrinology

paragraphs.text: unambiguous female phenotype and an androgen receptor gene mutation resulting in a premature stop codon was found to have a male gender identity, indicating that androgen signaling may not be essential for male gender identity development [1, 15–17].
paragraphs.heading: 39.2.2 Endocrinology

paragraphs.text: Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated that some sexually dimorphic brain structures are more closely aligned with gender identity than with physical sex characteristics in transgen der adults prior to treatment with genderaffriming hormones, with a similar trend in gender dysphoric youth [18–21]. A 2021 MRI study in transgender adults, prior to treatment with gender-affirming hormones, found that transgender people have a unique brain phe notype “rather than being merely shifted towards either end of the male-female spec trum” [22]. In addition, several functional brain studies in both transgender adolescents and adults (e.g., looking at responses to odor ous compounds or mental rotation tasks) found that patterns typically observed to be sexually dimorphic were more closely aligned with gender identity than with physical sex characteristics, even before treatment with gender-affirming sex hormones [23–25].
paragraphs.heading: 39.2.3 Neurobiology

paragraphs.text: The principal clinical manifestation for TGD children and adolescents is gender dysphoria. Gender dysphoria may be manifested in a vari ety of ways, including a strong desire to be treated as the experienced gender and not the gender associated with the sex designated at birth, to be rid of one’s sex characteristics, or a strong conviction that one has feelings and reac tions typical of the experienced gender [26].
paragraphs.heading: 39.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Children, as young as the age of 2 years, may present with gender incongruence, behav ing in traditional gender roles opposite to their assigned gender, asking to be called by a different name more suitable with their gender identity, or simply stating they are a “boy” or a “girl,” opposite to their assigned gender [27].

Not all children presenting with gender incon gruence will persist throughout their lifetimes. Studies examining persistence of gender iden tity found that only 20% of children who engaged in gender-nonconforming behavior before puberty will report a transgender gen der identity as an adult, with the main factor associated with persistence into adolescence and adulthood being increased intensity of gender-related dysphoria, assertion of gender identity cognitively versus affectively, and degree of social transition [28, 29]. What appears to be a relatively low rate of persis tence may be influenced by the fact that it may be difficult to distinguish gender expression from gender identity in young, prepubertal children, and that children whose behavior/ expression did not align with societal gender norms may not have been destined to have a transgender identity. Other studies have shown that children that experienced increased dysphoria in adolescence, starting between 10 and 13 years of age, were more likely to have a stable transgender identity [30].

With the onset of endogenous puberty, TGD adolescents may present with significant distress and worsening of gender dysphoria. The development of an adult version of a body that the young person experiences as “wrong” may represent the permanence of gender incongruence and can trigger negative psychosocial consequences, which may be exacerbated by complex trauma, societal stigma, violence, and discrimination [31, 32]. These psychosocial outcomes may include depression, anxiety, social isolation, selfharming behaviors, illicit drug use, high-risk sexual behavior, and suicidality. Compared with cisgender controls, TGD youth have been shown to have a twofold to threefold increased risk of internalizing disorders and lifethreatening behaviors [33]. Estimates of clini cally significant depressive symptoms or diagnoses have averaged in the range of 30–60%, and estimates of clinically significant anxiety symptoms or diagnoses have averaged in the range of 20–30%. Lifetime history of suicidal ideation (average range 30–50%), sui cide attempt (average range 15–30%), and nonsuicidal self-injury (average range 20–40%) also appear common [34].

Children and adolescents presenting with gender dysphoria may also have increased rates of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). In different studies, the incidence of a diagnosis of ASD ranged from 3% to 21.3% in TGD children and adolescents, higher than the prevalence of 1% of ASD in the general popu lation [35].

Primary care providers and mental health professionals are often the first point of con tact for TGD youth. It is important for these providers to recognize the possibility of gen der dysphoria and refer patients to clinical services with experience in the treatment of gender diverse people—ideally, a multidisci plinary care team that includes mental health, medical, social work, education/advocacy, and, if needed, legal support. It is essential that the determination of gender dysphoria in a youth/adolescent be made by a qualified mental health professional.
paragraphs.heading: 39.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: A letter of support from a mental health pro vider detailing gender history and evaluation of familial and social supports may be requested prior to proceeding with medical intervention. It is the medical provider’s responsibility to ensure that patients and their families understand not only the benefits but also the potential risks of medical interven tions as well as to establish a strategy for labo ratory and imaging surveillance of potential adverse physiologic effects. The World Profes sional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH) and the Endocrine Society have pub lished Standards of Care and Clinical Practice Guidelines, respectively, which are periodically updated [36, 37]. The Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline is cosponsored by the Pediat ric Endocrine Society, the European Society of Paediatric Endocrinology, WPATH, and a number of other professional societies.
paragraphs.heading: 39.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: For prepubertal children, who exhibit signifi cant gender dysphoria, a gender-affirmative approach is thought to have the best outcome [38]. In some cases, these children may insist on living as their experienced gender (social transition). Establishing care with a mental health gender specialist can assist families in providing optimal support to the child. At this stage, there are no medical therapies indi cated, as there are no significant levels of pubertal sex hormones. Additionally, the pre emptive treatment with puberty blockers (see below) prior to development of Tanner stage 2 of puberty is not advised [37].
paragraphs.heading: 39.5.1 Prepuberty

paragraphs.text: When TGD children enter Tanner stage 2 of puberty, there may be an increase in gender dysphoria. It is at this point that medical treatment can be considered, as long as there is adequate psychosocial support. Pioneering work by the Dutch has demonstrated that putting puberty “on hold” in early pubertal gender dysphoric youth can provide addi tional time to explore one’s gender identity working with a gender specialist and can pre vent the development of otherwise irrevers ible secondary sex characteristics [39]. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists (GnRHa) such as leuprolide and histrelin, considered generally reversible interventions, are the mainstay for pausing the progression of puberty in TGD youth. Confirmatory blood testing with ultrasensitive assays can be used in conjunction with the physical examination if the individual appears to be at the earliest stage of puberty. It should be noted that the emotional impact of early puberty has been considered to have diag nostic value in the determination of gender dysphoria [39]. Initiation and timing of pubertal blockers should be considered on a case-by-case basis after discussion with the patient and family about long-term goals and values.
paragraphs.heading: 39.5.2 Early Puberty

paragraphs.text: Studies have shown that TGD youth blocked at Tanner 2 will often seek phenotypic transi tion with gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT) with sex steroids estradiol or testos terone when they are older [40, 41]. While the Endocrine Society guidelines recommend that GAHT may be started by age 16, the guide lines also note that there may be compelling reasons to consider starting such treatment at an earlier age [37]. In addition to potential mental distress and social isolation by being kept in a prepubertal state until age 16 years, persisting in this hypogonadal state could have adverse consequences on bone mineral acquisition (see below).

There are currently limited outcomes data regarding the use of pubertal blockers and GAHT in TGD youth. However, in the past decade, numerous shorter-term studies and one medium-term study have demonstrated the positive, even life-saving, impact of gender-affirming medical care for TGD youth, as discussed below. The long-term risks of altering the hormonal milieu are unknown. Thus, long-term follow-up and further research are essential.
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: Medical intervention, as part of a multidisci plinary gender team approach in transgender adolescents, has been shown to have favorable mental health outcomes. A prospective Dutch study showed that after an average of nearly 2 years of GnRHa treatment, psychological functioning of adolescents diagnosed with gender identity disorder (a term that has now been replaced with “gender dysphoria” in DSM-5) had improved in many respects. Adolescents showed fewer behavioral and emotional problems, reported fewer depres sive symptoms, feelings of anxiety and anger remained stable (but did not decrease), and their general functioning improved [40]. A longer-term evaluation of the same cohort demonstrated that gender dysphoria and body image difficulties persisted through puberty suppression but remitted after the administra tion of gender-affirming hormones and gen der reassignment surgery. Psychological functioning improved steadily over time, resulting in rates of clinical problems that were indistinguishable from general popula tion samples, and quality of life, satisfaction
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.1 Mental Health

paragraphs.text: with life, and subjective happiness were comparable to same-age peers [45]. A more recent cross-sectional survey of more than 20,000 transgender adults demonstrated that individuals previously treated with GnRHa had a significantly lower odds of lifetime sui cidal ideation than those who wanted such treatment but did not receive it [46]. Another study examining youth receiving GAHT at a multidisciplinary program demonstrated sig nificant decreases in body dissatisfaction in response to gender-affirming medical care [34]. The largest observational study in the U.S. of the mental health impact of genderaffirming medical care in TGD adolescents and young adults (n = 315, age 12–20 years) demonstrated significant improvements in psychosocial functioning during 2 years of GAHT, with decreases in depression and anx iety and increases in appearance congruence (the degree to which physical characteristics align with gender identity), positive affect, and life satisfaction [47].

In prepubertal TGD children, where medi cal intervention is not indicated, it has been shown that socially transitioned children, who were supported in their identities, demon strated substantially lower rates of depression and anxiety as compared with children with gender identity disorder reported in previous studies. Rates of depression resembled popu lation averages, with only slightly elevated rates of anxiety symptoms. These findings suggest that familial support in general, or specifically via the decision to allow their chil dren to socially transition, may be associated with better mental health outcomes among transgender children [48].

Parental support is also beneficial in older age groups, as shown by a report from Ontario, Canada, that assessed the impact of the degree of parental support on mental health outcomes of transgender youth and young adults aged 16–24 years. This report demon strated that satisfaction with life and selfesteem was significantly greater in transgender youth whose parents were “very supportive” vs. those whose parents were “somewhat to not at all supportive,” with depression and suicide attempts significantly decreased among those with supportive parents [49, 50].

For adolescents undergoing gender-affirming care, the rates of discontinuation of such care are relatively low. In a 2020 study from the Netherlands, the vast majority of transgender adolescents who started GnRH agonist treat ment chose to go on to receive treatment with GAHT, with only 5 of 143 (3.5%) no longer wanting gender-affirming treatment [51]. A lon gitudinal study from the US and Canada dem onstrated that 5 years after their initial social transition, 94% of youth continued to identify as binary transgender, while 2.5% returned to a cisgender identity. Three and a half percent shifted to a nonbinary identity. Retransitioning to a cisgender identity was more common among youth whose initial social transition occurred before the age 6 years [52].
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.1.1 Retransitioning

paragraphs.text: Since peak bone mass, a major determinant of future adult fracture risk, is achieved dur ing puberty and young adulthood, medical treatment of TGD youth can potentially affect bone health. It is recommended that cli nicians obtain measures of bone density at baseline and annually while GnRHa are being used alone and at less frequent intervals after initiation of GAHT [37]. Any individual treated with a pubertal blocker should have careful monitoring of Vitamin D status (with supplementation if necessary), adequate intake of dietary calcium, and adequate weight-bearing exercise.
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.2 Bone Health

paragraphs.text: Bone density has been studied in individu als with delayed and early puberty. Delayed menarche is associated with increased fracture risk during childhood and adolescence, as well as osteoporosis in later life [53]. In delayed male puberty, data have also shown that low bone density is correlated with later timing of puberty [54]. There is evidence that age of onset of puberty does predict bone mass in young adulthood, although long-term followup is still needed in regards to fracture out comes [54, 55]. In patients with central precocious puberty treated with GnRHa, there is a decrease in bone mineral density (BMD) at onset of puberty suppression, but
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.2 Bone Health

paragraphs.text: levels rebound to control values after discon tinuation of GnRHa, which in turn allows resumption of endogenous puberty [56].
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.2 Bone Health

paragraphs.text: Since 2015, more studies have examined BMD in TGD youth, and while the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD) has provided guidance on how to interpret dual-energy X-ray absorp tiometry (DXA) in TGD adults [57], there remains no guidance on which BMD Z-score sex references to use in TGD youth [58]. Most literature to date has compared TGD youth and adults with sex designated at birth refer ences. In a U.S. cohort of early pubertal (Tanner Stage 2–3) TGD youth evaluated by DXA and quantitative computed tomography (QCT), a high percentage had low BMD prior to starting GnRHa, with 30% designated males at birth and 13% designated females at birth fulfilling the diagnosis of low BMD for age. In this cohort, TGD youth with low BMD had lower physical activity scores than those with normal BMD [59].
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.2 Bone Health

paragraphs.text: Longitudinal studies of skeletal trajecto ries of TGD youth receiving gender-affirming medical therapy are still relatively short term. Since the landmark study showing low pre treatment BMD by DXA and impaired bone mass accrual in transgender women who initi ated GnRHa in late puberty and received more than 5 years of estradiol therapy [60], other studies have focused on this potential adverse outcome [61–64]. These studies have shown lower BMD in transfeminine youth, with less concerning data in transmasculine youth. It is important to note that these longi tudinal studies of TGD youth on GAHT gen erally followed a model of later initiation of GAHT around 15–16 years of age.
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.2 Bone Health

paragraphs.text: A study investigating hip bone geometry in TGD individuals showed that those who initi ated GnRHa in early puberty had bone geom etry approximating their gender reference curves while those who initiated GnRHa in later or postpuberty had bone geometry closer to sex designated at birth reference curves [65]. These data suggest that TGD individuals who imitate treatment in early versus late puberty have distinct skeletal trajectories. Because of these complexities related to data interpretation and the still early years of
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.2 Bone Health

paragraphs.text: examining bone measures in TGD individuals who initiate gender-affirming medical therapy during puberty, long-term studies will be important in untangling and mitigating any potential increased future fracture risk.
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.2 Bone Health

paragraphs.text: TGD individuals often wish to preserve poten tial for fertility, and a discussion about the potential impact of pubertal blockers or GAHT on fertility and options for fertility preservation is an essential part of the informed consent process for all gender diverse individuals considering such care. If the use of GnRHa in early-pubertal TGD adolescents is later combined with GAHT, fertility will likely be compromised due to arrested gonadal mat uration. Currently, experimental harvesting of prepubertal gonadal tissue, cryopreservation, and in vitro maturation are being explored in other medical contexts [66, 67] and may be of benefit for fertility preservation in early puber tal transgender youth. Research to obtain arti ficial gametes through stem cells is also ongoing and could be a feasible option in the future, for those individuals who cannot or have not stored their own gametes [68]. A sig nificant advance in fertility preservation has been the demonstration of in vivo oocyte mat uration in a designated female at birth with a male gender identity. This adolescent under went treatment with a GnRHa at Tanner 2, resulting in pubertal suppression, and concur rently was treated a short course of ovarian stimulation with follitropin-α and human cho rionic gonadotropin [69]. With respect to TGD adolescents designated male at birth with a female gender identity who were treated with a GnRHa at Tanner 2, in vivo maturation of sperm has not yet been reported.
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.3 Fertility

paragraphs.text: In late pubertal or postpubertal TGD youth with mature gonads, fertility may be preserved via cryopreservation of sperm or oocytes, before initiating GAHT. Prolonged estrogen treatment results in reduction of testicular vol ume and has a suppressive effect on sperm motility and density, but these effects may be reversible. Testosterone treatment in most cases results in reversible amenorrhea, though ovar

ian follicles are not depleted. As such, hor monal interventions for transitioning do not exclude a possible pregnancy in transmasculine adults. In fact, it is important to counsel trans masculine adolescents that may engage in receptive vaginal sex that testosterone is not a reliable contraceptive. In cases where transmas culine individuals decide to retain ovaries and uterus, they may regain fertility after discon tinuing androgen therapy [68].

The first live birth after living uterine transplantation was reported in 2014 in a woman with congenital absence of the uterus (Rokitansky syndrome). The uterus was donated by a 61-year-old woman who had already had two successful pregnancies [70]. This type of procedure opens the possibility for assisted gestation for male-to-female transgender women, though not without sig nificant challenges, including the need for immunosuppressive therapy [71].

There are theoretical risks to the brain when using a GnRHa during adolescence, as puberty is thought to be associated with a further orga nizational period of brain development. GnRHa treatment in TGD adolescents did not appear to affect executive function, a cog nitive milestone associated with pubertal development [72]. However, after approxi mately 2 years of treatment with a GnRHa, lack of expected variation in white matter frac tional anisotropy and a nine-point drop in operational memory were demonstrated in a single case report in a TGD adolescent desig nated male at birth [73]. More research is needed to better assess potential adverse effects of GnRHa on the brain in transgender youth.
paragraphs.heading: 39.6.4 Brain

paragraphs.text: It is well-established that sex steroids have a significant effect on cardiovascular and meta bolic health [74]. Among TGD adults, greater cardiovascular morbidity has been reported with an increased risk of myocardial infarction
paragraphs.heading: Health

paragraphs.text: in both transgender women and transgender men compared to the general female popula tion [75]. TGD youth on GnRHa have been shown to have lower estimated insulin sensitiv ity and higher glycemic markers and body fat than cisgender controls with similar character istics [76]. TGD adolescents on GAHT have significant differences in body composition compared with cisgender controls, with a body composition intermediate between BMImatched cisgender males and cisgender females [77]. In a recent multicenter analysis, TGD youth treated with testosterone mono therapy or in combination with a GnRHa had higher odds of dyslipidemia and liver dysfunc tion than TGD youth who were not treated with GAHT [78]. TGD youth treated with tes tosterone alone had higher odds of overweight/ obesity and hypertension compared to those not treated with testosterone; neither GnRHa alone or estradiol monotherapy were associ ated with greater odds of cardiometabolicrelated diagnoses in this multicenter study [78].
paragraphs.heading: Health

paragraphs.text: Studies from the Netherlands, Belgium, and the U.S. have investigated the effects of GnRHa and GAHT on growth. In transgen der female adolescents, adult height after regular-dose estradiol (2 mg) treatment was close to target height. Compared to regulardose treatment, high-dose estradiol (6 mg) and ethinyl estradiol reduced adult height by 0.9 cm (95% CI, −0.9 cm to 2.8 cm) and 3.0 cm (95% CI, 0.2–5.8 cm), respectively [79]. In transgender male adolescents with a bone age ≤ 14 years, adult height was 3.9 ± 6.0 cm above midparental height and 3.0 ± 3.6 cm above predicted adult height at start of GnRHa [80]. A study examining growth in TGD youth in the first year of GnRHa treatment demonstrated that height velocity in this group was similar to that of prepubertal children. However, TGD youth who started GnRHa later in puberty (Tanner 4) had a height velocity below the prepuber tal range [81].

paragraphs.heading: 39.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: As awareness and scientific knowledge about the TGD population grow, pediatric endocri nologists and other clinicians (e.g., primary care, family practice, and adolescent medicine specialists) have seen increasing numbers of TGD youth, many of whom will ultimately desire medical or surgical transition. Identifying appropriate services, ideally in a multidisciplinary setting, is an important first step. Understanding that gender identity likely represents a complex interplay of biology, cul ture, and environment, and is influenced by more than just karyotype, hormones, and gen der of rearing, can lead to increased under standing of the challenges faced by TGD individuals and hopefully lead to increased acceptance and improved quality of life. Challenges to care include the fact that increas ing numbers of TGD youth who identify as nonbinary are presenting for gender-affirming care, for whom clinical practice guidelines do not currently exist. In addition, legislation banning access to gender-affirming care for minors has been proposed in numerous states in the U.S., in some cases criminalizing provid ers of such care [82]. While rigorous studies have shown that gender-affirming care is important in achieving positive mental health outcomes, data on the long-term impact on mental health and on physiologic effects on bone, fertility, brain, growth, and cardiometa bolic outcomes are still in progress. Long-term research is increasingly necessary to optimize medical and psychological care of TGD youth.

### 39.1 Introduction and Background

Recent literature and clinical experience have demonstrated that gender identity, described as one’s inner sense of self as male, female, or other nonbinary category, exists as a contin uum between maleness and femaleness. Furthermore, there is increasing evidence that gender identity is not merely a psychosocial construct but rather an entity governed by complex interactions among biology, environ ment, and culture. Gender identity is distinct from sex, the latter of which is categorized based on chromosomal and apparent physical characteristics such as genitalia. The general practice has been to assign sex at birth—and therefore, gender of rearing—based on phe notype, but growing awareness of potential discordance between the body and gender identity has transformed our understanding of what truly governs gender identity [1].

### 39

Transgender may be defined as a condition where one’s gender identity is not aligned or “congruent” with one’s physical sex character istics. Gender identity may also be nonbinary. Some individuals describe themselves as gen

der expansive, gender fluid, gender queer, or agender. “Cisgender” is a term that is used to describe an individual whose gender identity is in alignment with one’s physical sex charac teristics. It is important to recognize that gen der identity is distinct from sexual identity (sexual orientation). A person with any gen der identity can have any sexual orientation [1].

In 2013, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) removed the diagnosis of “gender identity disorder (GID)” from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Menal Disorders (DSM)-IV and replaced it with “gender dysphoria” in the updated DSM-5, described as a marked incongruence between one’s experienced/expressed gender and assigned gender of at least 6 months duration, which causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning [2]. This change in terminology underscores the con cept that a transgender identity, in and of itself, is no longer considered pathological and, instead, directs clinical concern to the dysphoria that may exist as a consequence of being TGD. It is anticipated that the DSM-6 will replace “gender dysphoria” with “gender incongruence,” acknowledging that not all TGD individuals experience dysphoria, espe cially if well-supported and affirmed in their gender identities.

The size of the TGD youth population is challenging to accurately ascertain, but survey-based studies have estimated that 0.7% to 2.7% of the teenagers in the United States identify as TGD [3–5]. Pediatric gender clinics worldwide have described increased referrals over the years, including the Netherlands [6, 7] and Canada [8].

### 39.2 Etiology

Gender identity is not simply a psychosocial construct but likely reflects a complex inter play of biology, culture, and environment [1]. Evidence for biological determinants of gen der identity comes from three biomedical dis ciplines such as genetics, endocrinology, and

neurology. Of note, the goal in reviewing such studies is not to develop a test to confirm someone’s gender identity nor to identify a mechanism that can be “fixed” to prevent gen der diversity. Rather, it is hoped that an appre ciation that biology contributes to gender identity development can lead to destigamati zation and greater acceptance for gender diverse persons [1].

### 39.2.1 Genetics

Evidence implicating genetics as a contribut ing factor to gender identity development is derived from studies of twins as well as from studies of polymorphisms in candidate genes that might be more prevalent in transgender persons versus cisgender controls. A literature review in 2012 focused on twins with what was then known as GID [9]. Of 23 pairs of mono zygotic female or male twins, nine pairs (39.1%) were concordant for GID, while there was no concordance for GID in 21 same-sex dizygotic female and male twin pairs or in seven opposite-sex twin pairs [9]. While these studies suggest that DNA does play a role in gender identity development, the fact that concordance for being transgender was only 39.1% in this study of identical twins may reflect epigenetic changes or the fact that indi viduals may “come out” as transgender at any age, even late in life. Studies attempting to identify polymorphisms in candidate genes that might be more prevalent in transgender versus cisgender persons have been inconsis tent. For example, a 2009 study from Japan did not find any significant associations between a transgender identity and polymor phisms in five candidate genes (encoding the androgen receptor, CYP19, ER-α, ER-β, and the progesterone receptor) [10]. However, a 2019 study from the U.S. and Australia in 380 transgender women and 344 cisgender male controls investigated repeat length polymor phisms or single nucleotide polymorphisms in 12 sex hormone signaling genes [11]. In this study, significant associations were identified between gender dysphoria and a number of alleles and genotypes, including an overrepre sentation of several allele combinations

involving the androgen receptor in transgen der women [11]. An association between poly morphisms in the estrogen receptor α gene (ESR1) promoter and gender incongruence in transgender males was reported in a 2020 study from Spain [12].

### 39.2.2 Endocrinology

While most transgender individuals do not have a difference in sex development (DSD), studies of patients with DSDs support a role of hormones—prenatal (and perhaps postna tal) androgens, in particular—in gender iden tity development. However, the hormonal environment is not likely to be the only deter minant of gender identity, given that most transgender individuals do not have any dis cernable evidence of hormonal abnormalities (though there may have been some variations in prenatal hormone secretion or sensitivity that are not readily apparent from examina tion of the external genitalia).

Individuals with virilizing congenital adre nal hyperplasia (CAH) represent a population in which the early hormonal environment of 46,XX individuals is largely androgenic, due to various defects in the steroidogenesis path way. Review of the literature has shown that in a case series of 250 46,XX adult individuals with virilizing CAH caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency that were raised female, nearly 95% were identified as females. However, 5.2% had significant gender dysphoria or cross-gender identification, which is significantly higher than the estimated prevalence of female-tomale transgender individuals in the general population [13]. There was, however, no cor relation between degree of genital virilization and gender identity outcome [13]. A study in youth with virilizing 21-hydroxylase-deficient CAH demonstrated that 12.8% of 46,XX individuals demonstrated cross-gender identi fication independent of gender behavior [14]. A variety of other hormonal and nonhor monal DSDs, particularly in 46,XY individu als, support some role of prenatal/postnatal androgens in gender identity development; however, an individual with complete andro gen insensitivity syndrome associated with an

### 39.2.3 Neurobiology

Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated that some sexually dimorphic brain structures are more closely aligned with gender identity than with physical sex characteristics in transgen der adults prior to treatment with genderaffriming hormones, with a similar trend in gender dysphoric youth [18–21]. A 2021 MRI study in transgender adults, prior to treatment with gender-affirming hormones, found that transgender people have a unique brain phe notype “rather than being merely shifted towards either end of the male-female spec trum” [22]. In addition, several functional brain studies in both transgender adolescents and adults (e.g., looking at responses to odor ous compounds or mental rotation tasks) found that patterns typically observed to be sexually dimorphic were more closely aligned with gender identity than with physical sex characteristics, even before treatment with gender-affirming sex hormones [23–25].

### 39.3 Clinical Presentation

The principal clinical manifestation for TGD children and adolescents is gender dysphoria. Gender dysphoria may be manifested in a vari ety of ways, including a strong desire to be treated as the experienced gender and not the gender associated with the sex designated at birth, to be rid of one’s sex characteristics, or a strong conviction that one has feelings and reac tions typical of the experienced gender [26].

### 39

Children, as young as the age of 2 years, may present with gender incongruence, behav ing in traditional gender roles opposite to their assigned gender, asking to be called by a different name more suitable with their gender identity, or simply stating they are a “boy” or a “girl,” opposite to their assigned gender [27].

Not all children presenting with gender incon gruence will persist throughout their lifetimes. Studies examining persistence of gender iden tity found that only 20% of children who engaged in gender-nonconforming behavior before puberty will report a transgender gen der identity as an adult, with the main factor associated with persistence into adolescence and adulthood being increased intensity of gender-related dysphoria, assertion of gender identity cognitively versus affectively, and degree of social transition [28, 29]. What appears to be a relatively low rate of persis tence may be influenced by the fact that it may be difficult to distinguish gender expression from gender identity in young, prepubertal children, and that children whose behavior/ expression did not align with societal gender norms may not have been destined to have a transgender identity. Other studies have shown that children that experienced increased dysphoria in adolescence, starting between 10 and 13 years of age, were more likely to have a stable transgender identity [30].

With the onset of endogenous puberty, TGD adolescents may present with significant distress and worsening of gender dysphoria. The development of an adult version of a body that the young person experiences as “wrong” may represent the permanence of gender incongruence and can trigger negative psychosocial consequences, which may be exacerbated by complex trauma, societal stigma, violence, and discrimination [31, 32]. These psychosocial outcomes may include depression, anxiety, social isolation, selfharming behaviors, illicit drug use, high-risk sexual behavior, and suicidality. Compared with cisgender controls, TGD youth have been shown to have a twofold to threefold increased risk of internalizing disorders and lifethreatening behaviors [33]. Estimates of clini cally significant depressive symptoms or diagnoses have averaged in the range of 30–60%, and estimates of clinically significant anxiety symptoms or diagnoses have averaged in the range of 20–30%. Lifetime history of suicidal ideation (average range 30–50%), sui cide attempt (average range 15–30%), and nonsuicidal self-injury (average range 20–40%) also appear common [34].

### 39.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

Primary care providers and mental health professionals are often the first point of con tact for TGD youth. It is important for these providers to recognize the possibility of gen der dysphoria and refer patients to clinical services with experience in the treatment of gender diverse people—ideally, a multidisci plinary care team that includes mental health, medical, social work, education/advocacy, and, if needed, legal support. It is essential that the determination of gender dysphoria in a youth/adolescent be made by a qualified mental health professional.

### 39.5 Treatment

A letter of support from a mental health pro vider detailing gender history and evaluation of familial and social supports may be requested prior to proceeding with medical intervention. It is the medical provider’s responsibility to ensure that patients and their families understand not only the benefits but also the potential risks of medical interven tions as well as to establish a strategy for labo ratory and imaging surveillance of potential adverse physiologic effects. The World Profes sional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH) and the Endocrine Society have pub lished Standards of Care and Clinical Practice Guidelines, respectively, which are periodically updated [36, 37]. The Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline is cosponsored by the Pediat ric Endocrine Society, the European Society of Paediatric Endocrinology, WPATH, and a number of other professional societies.

### 39.5.1 Prepuberty

For prepubertal children, who exhibit signifi cant gender dysphoria, a gender-affirmative approach is thought to have the best outcome [38]. In some cases, these children may insist on living as their experienced gender (social transition). Establishing care with a mental health gender specialist can assist families in providing optimal support to the child. At this stage, there are no medical therapies indi cated, as there are no significant levels of pubertal sex hormones. Additionally, the pre emptive treatment with puberty blockers (see below) prior to development of Tanner stage 2 of puberty is not advised [37].

### 39.5.2 Early Puberty

When TGD children enter Tanner stage 2 of puberty, there may be an increase in gender dysphoria. It is at this point that medical treatment can be considered, as long as there is adequate psychosocial support. Pioneering work by the Dutch has demonstrated that putting puberty “on hold” in early pubertal gender dysphoric youth can provide addi tional time to explore one’s gender identity working with a gender specialist and can pre vent the development of otherwise irrevers ible secondary sex characteristics [39]. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists (GnRHa) such as leuprolide and histrelin, considered generally reversible interventions, are the mainstay for pausing the progression of puberty in TGD youth. Confirmatory blood testing with ultrasensitive assays can be used in conjunction with the physical examination if the individual appears to be at the earliest stage of puberty. It should be noted that the emotional impact of early puberty has been considered to have diag nostic value in the determination of gender dysphoria [39]. Initiation and timing of pubertal blockers should be considered on a case-by-case basis after discussion with the patient and family about long-term goals and values.

### 39.6 Outcomes and Possible

### Complications

There are currently limited outcomes data regarding the use of pubertal blockers and GAHT in TGD youth. However, in the past decade, numerous shorter-term studies and one medium-term study have demonstrated the positive, even life-saving, impact of gender-affirming medical care for TGD youth, as discussed below. The long-term risks of altering the hormonal milieu are unknown. Thus, long-term follow-up and further research are essential.

### 39.6.1 Mental Health

Medical intervention, as part of a multidisci plinary gender team approach in transgender adolescents, has been shown to have favorable mental health outcomes. A prospective Dutch study showed that after an average of nearly 2 years of GnRHa treatment, psychological functioning of adolescents diagnosed with gender identity disorder (a term that has now been replaced with “gender dysphoria” in DSM-5) had improved in many respects. Adolescents showed fewer behavioral and emotional problems, reported fewer depres sive symptoms, feelings of anxiety and anger remained stable (but did not decrease), and their general functioning improved [40]. A longer-term evaluation of the same cohort demonstrated that gender dysphoria and body image difficulties persisted through puberty suppression but remitted after the administra tion of gender-affirming hormones and gen der reassignment surgery. Psychological functioning improved steadily over time, resulting in rates of clinical problems that were indistinguishable from general popula tion samples, and quality of life, satisfaction

with life, and subjective happiness were comparable to same-age peers [45]. A more recent cross-sectional survey of more than 20,000 transgender adults demonstrated that individuals previously treated with GnRHa had a significantly lower odds of lifetime sui cidal ideation than those who wanted such treatment but did not receive it [46]. Another study examining youth receiving GAHT at a multidisciplinary program demonstrated sig nificant decreases in body dissatisfaction in response to gender-affirming medical care [34]. The largest observational study in the U.S. of the mental health impact of genderaffirming medical care in TGD adolescents and young adults (n = 315, age 12–20 years) demonstrated significant improvements in psychosocial functioning during 2 years of GAHT, with decreases in depression and anx iety and increases in appearance congruence (the degree to which physical characteristics align with gender identity), positive affect, and life satisfaction [47].

In prepubertal TGD children, where medi cal intervention is not indicated, it has been shown that socially transitioned children, who were supported in their identities, demon strated substantially lower rates of depression and anxiety as compared with children with gender identity disorder reported in previous studies. Rates of depression resembled popu lation averages, with only slightly elevated rates of anxiety symptoms. These findings suggest that familial support in general, or specifically via the decision to allow their chil dren to socially transition, may be associated with better mental health outcomes among transgender children [48].

Parental support is also beneficial in older age groups, as shown by a report from Ontario, Canada, that assessed the impact of the degree of parental support on mental health outcomes of transgender youth and young adults aged 16–24 years. This report demon strated that satisfaction with life and selfesteem was significantly greater in transgender youth whose parents were “very supportive” vs. those whose parents were “somewhat to not at all supportive,” with depression and suicide attempts significantly decreased among those with supportive parents [49, 50].

### 39.6.1.1 Retransitioning

For adolescents undergoing gender-affirming care, the rates of discontinuation of such care are relatively low. In a 2020 study from the Netherlands, the vast majority of transgender adolescents who started GnRH agonist treat ment chose to go on to receive treatment with GAHT, with only 5 of 143 (3.5%) no longer wanting gender-affirming treatment [51]. A lon gitudinal study from the US and Canada dem onstrated that 5 years after their initial social transition, 94% of youth continued to identify as binary transgender, while 2.5% returned to a cisgender identity. Three and a half percent shifted to a nonbinary identity. Retransitioning to a cisgender identity was more common among youth whose initial social transition occurred before the age 6 years [52].

### 39.6.2 Bone Health

Since peak bone mass, a major determinant of future adult fracture risk, is achieved dur ing puberty and young adulthood, medical treatment of TGD youth can potentially affect bone health. It is recommended that cli nicians obtain measures of bone density at baseline and annually while GnRHa are being used alone and at less frequent intervals after initiation of GAHT [37]. Any individual treated with a pubertal blocker should have careful monitoring of Vitamin D status (with supplementation if necessary), adequate intake of dietary calcium, and adequate weight-bearing exercise.

Bone density has been studied in individu als with delayed and early puberty. Delayed menarche is associated with increased fracture risk during childhood and adolescence, as well as osteoporosis in later life [53]. In delayed male puberty, data have also shown that low bone density is correlated with later timing of puberty [54]. There is evidence that age of onset of puberty does predict bone mass in young adulthood, although long-term followup is still needed in regards to fracture out comes [54, 55]. In patients with central precocious puberty treated with GnRHa, there is a decrease in bone mineral density (BMD) at onset of puberty suppression, but

levels rebound to control values after discon tinuation of GnRHa, which in turn allows resumption of endogenous puberty [56].

Since 2015, more studies have examined BMD in TGD youth, and while the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD) has provided guidance on how to interpret dual-energy X-ray absorp tiometry (DXA) in TGD adults [57], there remains no guidance on which BMD Z-score sex references to use in TGD youth [58]. Most literature to date has compared TGD youth and adults with sex designated at birth refer ences. In a U.S. cohort of early pubertal (Tanner Stage 2–3) TGD youth evaluated by DXA and quantitative computed tomography (QCT), a high percentage had low BMD prior to starting GnRHa, with 30% designated males at birth and 13% designated females at birth fulfilling the diagnosis of low BMD for age. In this cohort, TGD youth with low BMD had lower physical activity scores than those with normal BMD [59].

Longitudinal studies of skeletal trajecto ries of TGD youth receiving gender-affirming medical therapy are still relatively short term. Since the landmark study showing low pre treatment BMD by DXA and impaired bone mass accrual in transgender women who initi ated GnRHa in late puberty and received more than 5 years of estradiol therapy [60], other studies have focused on this potential adverse outcome [61–64]. These studies have shown lower BMD in transfeminine youth, with less concerning data in transmasculine youth. It is important to note that these longi tudinal studies of TGD youth on GAHT gen erally followed a model of later initiation of GAHT around 15–16 years of age.

A study investigating hip bone geometry in TGD individuals showed that those who initi ated GnRHa in early puberty had bone geom etry approximating their gender reference curves while those who initiated GnRHa in later or postpuberty had bone geometry closer to sex designated at birth reference curves [65]. These data suggest that TGD individuals who imitate treatment in early versus late puberty have distinct skeletal trajectories. ### 39.6.3 Fertility

TGD individuals often wish to preserve poten tial for fertility, and a discussion about the potential impact of pubertal blockers or GAHT on fertility and options for fertility preservation is an essential part of the informed consent process for all gender diverse individuals considering such care. If the use of GnRHa in early-pubertal TGD adolescents is later combined with GAHT, fertility will likely be compromised due to arrested gonadal mat uration. Currently, experimental harvesting of prepubertal gonadal tissue, cryopreservation, and in vitro maturation are being explored in other medical contexts [66, 67] and may be of benefit for fertility preservation in early puber tal transgender youth. Research to obtain arti ficial gametes through stem cells is also ongoing and could be a feasible option in the future, for those individuals who cannot or have not stored their own gametes [68]. A sig nificant advance in fertility preservation has been the demonstration of in vivo oocyte mat uration in a designated female at birth with a male gender identity. This adolescent under went treatment with a GnRHa at Tanner 2, resulting in pubertal suppression, and concur rently was treated a short course of ovarian stimulation with follitropin-α and human cho rionic gonadotropin [69]. With respect to TGD adolescents designated male at birth with a female gender identity who were treated with a GnRHa at Tanner 2, in vivo maturation of sperm has not yet been reported.

Prolonged estrogen treatment results in reduction of testicular vol ume and has a suppressive effect on sperm motility and density, but these effects may be reversible. Testosterone treatment in most cases results in reversible amenorrhea, though ovar

In cases where transmas culine individuals decide to retain ovaries and uterus, they may regain fertility after discon tinuing androgen therapy [68].

The first live birth after living uterine transplantation was reported in 2014 in a woman with congenital absence of the uterus (Rokitansky syndrome). The uterus was donated by a 61-year-old woman who had already had two successful pregnancies [70]. This type of procedure opens the possibility for assisted gestation for male-to-female transgender women, though not without sig nificant challenges, including the need for immunosuppressive therapy [71].

### 39.6.4 Brain

There are theoretical risks to the brain when using a GnRHa during adolescence, as puberty is thought to be associated with a further orga nizational period of brain development. GnRHa treatment in TGD adolescents did not appear to affect executive function, a cog nitive milestone associated with pubertal development [72]. However, after approxi mately 2 years of treatment with a GnRHa, lack of expected variation in white matter frac tional anisotropy and a nine-point drop in operational memory were demonstrated in a single case report in a TGD adolescent desig nated male at birth [73]. More research is needed to better assess potential adverse effects of GnRHa on the brain in transgender youth.
